title: Blessings of the heart
hook: respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, and being easy to correct

segments.voice: Yesterday: the blessings at home, and your line, a blessing. Did you do your small act of care? Today ends the week, and the poem turns inward. Day five hundred ninety-five.

Someone at work points out a mistake in your report. Not cruelly; it's just wrong. And there's a tiny moment, maybe half a second, before you answer. A lot rides on that half second. Do you bristle, explain, defend? Or do you say: oh, you're right, thanks? The Mangala Sutta has a word for the second answer, and it calls it one of the highest blessings. So far the poem has covered company, learning, home and work. Now it reaches the qualities inside a person. Today: blessings of the heart.
screen: `A MISTAKE IN YOUR REPORT.` → `HALF A SECOND TO ANSWER.` → `THE POEM TURNS INWARD.`

segments.voice: The verse goes: respect and humility, contentment and gratitude, and hearing the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Then the next: patience, being easy to correct, seeing those who live a holy life, and talking about the teaching at the right time. That is the highest blessing. Look at gratitude. The Pali is kataññuta. Kata, what was done; ññu, knowing. Gratitude is knowing what has been done for you. Not a feeling you have to manufacture. A kind of seeing: someone made this meal, someone taught me to read, someone kept the lights on. The Buddha elsewhere says that grateful people, those who know what has been done for them, are rare in the world. And look at being easy to correct, sovacassata. Literally, being good to speak to. The person you can tell something to without a fight. It sits right next to patience, and it's the half-second answer from the report. These are blessings because they open a person. Contentment leaves room. Humility lets teaching in. Gratitude lets you see. Look back at the week. The sage with no fear-built ties. The jewel, chanted on a truth. The smell of deeds, not of food. A friend you can rest on. Then wise company, home, and now the heart. Again and again this week, the good thing turned out to be something a person does or is, not something that happens to them.
screen: `RESPECT, HUMILITY, CONTENTMENT` · `GRATITUDE: KNOWING WHAT WAS DONE` · `EASY TO CORRECT, PATIENT` · `A WEEK OF WHAT A PERSON DOES` · then, large: `GRATITUDE IS A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gratitude as seeing. Sit and settle. Look at one thing near you: a chair, a cup, the clothes you're wearing. Now trace what was done for it to be here. Someone grew the cotton, someone sewed, someone drove the truck, someone stocked the shelf. Don't force a warm feeling. Just know what was done. Then let one person who did something for you come to mind, and know that too. Rest in that knowing. The bell holds the time.
Kataññuta, gratitude. In the Mangala Sutta: respect, humility, contentment, patience and being easy to correct, the blessings that open a person. Today's word.
Your line: gratitude is a blessing. Tell one person today exactly what they did for you, not just thanks, but the thing itself. Day five hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice gratitude through daily chanting, offerings to monastics and teachers, and merit-dedication ceremonies for parents and ancestors.

fork.setup: a coworker points out a real mistake in your work. you have half a second. what does the blessings poem call the good answer?
fork.reveal: sovacassata, being easy to speak to and correct, is one of the highest blessings, listed right beside patience.

original.note: Pali kataññuta: gratitude, literally knowing what has been done (for you).

trapdoor: what you thought: gratitude is a warm feeling of thanks.
what it means: kataññuta is knowing what has been done for you: a kind of seeing.
what a scholar hears: AN 2.118 calls the grateful person (katavedi kataññu) rare in the world; in the Mangala Sutta gratitude sits with reverence, humility and contentment.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 2.4, Mangala Sutta, verses on reverence, gratitude, patience and correction
Anguttara Nikaya 2.118: two persons rare in the world

notes: Sn 2.4 paraphrased. Confirm the verses: garavo ca nivato ca santutthi ca kataññuta, kalena dhammassavanam; khanti ca sovacassata, samananañca dassanam, kalena dhammasakaccha.
Confirm the AN reference for 'two persons rare in the world' (the one who does a favor first and the grateful one); numbering varies by edition (AN 2.118 or AN 2.11.x).

Pronunciation of kataññuta with the palatal ñ; confirm the 'say' field.
